subject: space
title: Moon Phases
name: Moon Phases
system: Moon · orbiting Earth, lit by the Sun
tagline: The Moon never changes shape — only how much lit side faces us does
summary: The Moon doesn't make its own light, and it doesn't actually change shape — half of it is always lit by the Sun, exactly like Earth always has a day side and a night side. What changes across about 29.5 days is how much of that lit half happens to be facing Earth as the Moon orbits us, which is exactly what the phase wheel tracks.

keyFacts.label: Full phase cycle (synodic month)
keyFacts.value: ~29.5 days — slightly longer, because Earth also moved around the Sun meanwhile

keyFacts.label: New Moon
keyFacts.value: Moon is between Earth and Sun — its lit side faces away from us entirely

keyFacts.label: Full Moon
keyFacts.value: Moon is opposite the Sun — its whole lit side faces Earth

keyFacts.label: Half the Moon
keyFacts.value: Is always lit by the Sun, no matter what phase we see

keyFacts.label: Common misconception
keyFacts.value: Phases are NOT caused by Earth's shadow — that's what an eclipse is, and it's rare

whyItMatters: Mixing up moon phases with eclipses is one of the most common mistakes in astronomy — this simulation makes the real cause (simple geometry, not a shadow) impossible to miss, since you can watch the same sunlight source stay fixed while only the Moon's angle to Earth changes.
didYouKnow: Because the Moon is tidally locked to Earth, we always see the same face of it no matter what phase it's in — the changing shape is entirely about lighting angle, never about the Moon turning to show us a different side.
conditions: Half of the Moon is always sunlit
The Moon orbits Earth roughly every 27.3 days
The visible lit fraction depends only on the Sun-Earth-Moon angle
compareReason: Phases and eclipses are both about Sun-Earth-Moon geometry and get confused constantly — comparing them side by side makes the real difference obvious: phases happen every month from ordinary angles, eclipses need a rare, near-perfect straight line.
